name: Fat burner supplements

lead: Fat burners are over-the-counter supplement blends, often built around caffeine-type stimulants and plant extracts, sold to raise metabolism or cut body fat. Users take them to speed fat loss and get a leaner, more defined look.

The chain: the marketed effect is higher energy expenditure and lower appetite, often called thermogenic, which adds up to a bigger calorie deficit. Mechanisms differ by ingredient and are not established for the blends as sold. The sources reviewed contain no efficacy data for the category as a whole, and individual ingredients vary widely in how much research exists.

paras: People take capsules or powders, usually in the morning or before training, alongside a calorie-controlled diet and exercise. Blends vary widely between products, so routines and ingredients differ.

Wikipedia's supplement overview reports that weight-loss products are a leading cause of supplement liver injury, that multi-ingredient products have been linked to more adverse events, and that many products with undeclared drugs were sold for weight loss. Stimulants can bring jitters and psychiatric effects. In the US they are sold without pre-market approval.

angle.text: Users take multi-ingredient stimulant blends to speed fat loss and get a leaner, more defined look. The blends aim to raise energy use and lower appetite, widening the calorie deficit. Blends vary widely between products, and efficacy has not been established at the category level.

lead: Fat burner supplements are over-the-counter products, usually multi-ingredient stimulant blends, marketed to increase metabolic rate, curb appetite or reduce body fat. People take them while dieting to get leaner and show more muscle definition and a sharper face and waistline. They fall within the broader category of weight-loss dietary supplements, which in the United States are regulated under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA): no pre-market approval is required and the FDA generally acts only after a product is on sale.[1]

Common ingredients are caffeine and plant extracts, and in the past ephedra; in bodybuilding, thermogenics are used to try to raise basal metabolic rate and overall energy expenditure.[2] The classic ECA stack of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin was associated with roughly 4 to 6 kg of weight loss in the figures summarised by Wikipedia's article on anti-obesity medication, and ephedra supplements were banned in the US in 2004.[3][4]

The Wikipedia overview of dietary supplements reports that weight-loss and bodybuilding products most often cause liver injury among supplements, that green tea catechins are among the most implicated ingredients, and that products with multiple ingredients have caused more adverse events than single-ingredient ones.[1]
infobox: Liver injury, undeclared drugs, psychiatric effects

paras: The term covers a wide range of products sold in capsule, tablet or powder form. Stimulant-based stacks are the form most associated with the phrase in looksmaxxing and fitness communities. Thermogenics in general are agents used in bodybuilding to try to raise basal metabolic rate; caffeine and ephedrine are common ingredients, and the stronger compound 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is described as able to cause death by hyperthermia.[2]

Ephedra, from Ephedra sinica, contains ephedrine and related alkaloids that raise heart rate, blood pressure and metabolism, and it was popular as a weight-loss and athletic aid, sometimes with caffeine and aspirin. Adverse event reports accumulated, including heart attacks, strokes and deaths, and potency varied as much as tenfold between lots of one brand.[4] The death of baseball pitcher Steve Bechler in 2003, where a medical examiner said ephedra toxicity played a significant role, intensified pressure for regulation.[4]

The FDA banned dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids in 2004, the ban was upheld on appeal in 2006, and the Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 2007.[4] Wikipedia's summary of anti-obesity medications reports ephedra's effect at about 0.9 kg per month more than placebo, ECA combinations associated with roughly 4 to 6 kg of loss, and a meta-analysis of ephedrine-containing products with an average loss of about 1.9 kg.[3]

Under DSHEA, supplements are treated as food. Manufacturers are responsible for confirming safety, disease claims are prohibited, and structure/function claims are allowed with a disclaimer.[1] Good manufacturing practice rules took effect in 2007, and the FDA can issue warning letters, seize products and seek recalls.[1]

A study covering 2007 to 2016 identified 776 supplements containing undeclared pharmaceutical drugs, 86% of which were marketed for weight loss or sexual performance.[1] US Government Accountability Office data for 2008 to 2011 recorded 6,307 supplement-related adverse event reports, with combination products linked to more events than single-ingredient ones.[1]

Liver injury from herbal and dietary supplements accounts for roughly 16 to 20% of supplement-related injuries, and weight-loss products most often cause hepatocellular injury with jaundice. Weight-loss supplements have also been linked to adverse psychiatric effects and to interactions with prescription drugs.[1]

On T Nation, 'fat burners' is used both for over-the-counter blends and, by some posters, for prescription compounds: one competitor describes T3 and clenbuterol as the fat burners he used in contest prep.[5] Supplement advertising is itself a topic; in a thread about a fat-burner ad campaign, a poster remarked that every fat burner claims to burn fat, and another thread jokes about influencer discount codes attached to a supposed single fat-burner transformation.[6][7]

No studies found for fat burner supplements as a defined product category. Trials of individual ingredients exist and are covered in the relevant ingredient articles. Reviews of ephedrine-containing products are summarised above.[3]

lore.intro: Fat burners are discussed in fitness forums as cutting aids and as a heavily marketed category.[6][7][5]
